blocks.prompt: 14. Find the \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of the progression \(\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)^{10}, \left(\frac{10}{7}\right)^{10}, \left(\frac{17}{7}\right)^{10}, \ldots\) Is the progression an A.P.? Is it infinite?
blocks.explanation:
Every term is a base raised to the power 10, and the bases follow a pattern.
We must find \(a_n\), then answer two yes/no questions.
Plan: find the \(n\)th base, raise it to the power 10; test the gaps between terms; look at how the list ends.
steps:
Given: \(\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)^{10}, \left(\frac{10}{7}\right)^{10}, \left(\frac{17}{7}\right)^{10}, \ldots\)
To find: \(a_n\); whether it is an A.P.; whether it is infinite.
Method: The tops of the bases, \(3, 10, 17, \ldots\), form an A.P., so we can write the \(n\)th base.

Find the nth base
\[3 + (n - 1)7 = 7n - 4\]
\[n\text{th base} = \dfrac{7n - 4}{7}\]
Why: The tops are an A.P. with first term 3 and \(d = 7\); the bottom is always 7.

Write the nth term
\[a_n = \left(\dfrac{7n - 4}{7}\right)^{10}\]
Why: Each term is its base to the power 10. Check: \(n = 1\) gives \(\left(\frac{3}{7}\right)^{10}\).

Is it an A.P.?
\[a_2 - a_1 \approx 35.4\]
\[a_3 - a_2 \approx 7101.5\]
Why: In an A.P. consecutive differences are equal. These are not, so the progression is not an A.P. The bases are in A.P., but raising them to the power 10 destroys the equal gaps.

Is it infinite?
\[a_n \text{ is defined for every } n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\]
Why: The list ends with '...' and no last term, so the terms go on for ever.
blocks.final_answer: \(a_n = \left(\frac{7n - 4}{7}\right)^{10}\); it is not an A.P.; yes, it is infinite.
